title: Three Indian Sailors Are Dead. India Says the US Navy Has Struck Three Ships With Indian Crews This Week.
excerpt: India summoned the American chargé d'affaires and demanded the attacks stop. The US blockade of Iranian oil has now killed its first civilians — all three were Indian.
body:
Three Indian sailors are dead after the US military struck an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman on Wednesday. India confirmed the deaths on Thursday and demanded that America stop attacking ships carrying Indian crews.

The Palau-flagged tanker MT Settebello was hit with precision munitions fired into its engine room after the crew "repeatedly failed to comply with directions from American forces," according to US Central Command. The ship was carrying 24 Indian nationals. Twenty-one were rescued by the Omani Navy after the vessel reported an engine fire. Three did not survive.

Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal called the deaths "deeply unfortunate" and said he had directed officials to repatriate the survivors and return the remains of the dead. Family members of one victim, Shivanand Chaurasia, told reporters he had gone to sea about nine months ago and had called his father earlier in the week to say everything was fine.

Three Ships in Five Days

The Settebello was not an isolated strike. India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed that the US Navy has attacked three ships with Indian crews this week alone.

The first was the Marivex oil tanker, disabled with precision munitions on Monday. On Thursday — hours after India summoned the American chargé d'affaires in New Delhi to protest — the US struck a third vessel, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged Jalveer. A US aircraft fired two Hellfire missiles into the Jalveer's engine room. All 20 Indian crew members survived.

"These attacks must cease and end," Jaiswal told reporters. "We also call for dialogue and diplomacy so that we can have an early return to peace and stability in the region."

Only the Marivex was under US sanctions. The Settebello and Jalveer were not.

The Blockade

The US began its maritime blockade on April 13, after Iran effectively shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow passage through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply flows. The blockade has since disabled nine non-compliant vessels, redirected 135 others, and allowed 42 humanitarian aid ships to pass.

The targets include Iranian vessels and so-called shadow fleet tankers — older ships without Western insurance, sailing under flags of convenience to transport sanctioned oil. Central Command says crews are given warnings before strikes. Critics, including Indian maritime unions, argue that disabling a ship with missiles while crew are aboard is a disproportionate response.

Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen's Union of India, questioned why authorities could not detain vessels instead of firing on them. He also expressed scepticism about US claims that they were unaware of the crew's nationalities.

India's 300,000 Sailors

India has more than 300,000 sailors working in global shipping fleets, according to government data. Many serve on the very type of vessel now being targeted — older tankers operating in contested waters under third-country flags.

Jaiswal emphasised that the attacked ships are not Indian-owned. But the crews are overwhelmingly Indian. The distinction between flag state, vessel owner, and crew nationality is a legal abstraction that matters little to the families of the dead.

The Indian government has not directly accused the United States of negligence or violation of international law, but the tone has sharpened notably. Summoning a diplomat is a strong signal in Indian foreign policy — reserved for moments of genuine anger, not routine concern.

A Deepening Strain

The tanker strikes come at a particularly fraught moment in US-India relations. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump are scheduled to meet bilaterally at the G7 summit in France next week. Trade tariffs, H-1B visa fees, and defence cooperation were already on the agenda. The deaths of three Indian sailors have now added a visceral new dimension.

India has maintained a neutral posture in the Iran-US conflict, calling for dialogue while protecting its own energy interests. It has not joined the US blockade and has not condemned Iran's closure of the strait. But the deaths of Indian civilians in American military operations push the equilibrium.

For the Indian diaspora, the incident crystallises a broader anxiety: Indian workers remain among the most exposed in global conflict zones — from shipping lanes in the Gulf to construction sites in war-adjacent countries — and the protections available to them often amount to consular statements after the fact.

The investigation into the Settebello strike is ongoing. The US Embassy in New Delhi said it was in contact with the Indian government but declined to comment further.

author: Diaspora Desk
